articles.title: DP World appoints two independent non-executive directors
articles.summary: DP World has appointed Amer Abdulrahim Kazim and Iman Al Qasim as Independent Non-Executive Directors to its Board, effective immediately. The global ports and logistics operator announced the appointments on October 26, 2026. Both executives bring extensive experience in finance, corporate governance, human capital...
articles.body: DP World has appointed Amer Abdulrahim Kazim and Iman Al Qasim as Independent Non-Executive Directors to its Board, effective immediately. The global ports and logistics operator announced the appointments on October 26, 2026. Both executives bring extensive experience in finance, corporate governance, human capital and organisational transformation. According to DP World, the appointments will strengthen the Board’s expertise and support the company’s long-term strategic objectives. New directors bring financial and leadership experience Amer Abdulrahim Kazim currently serves as Group Chief Audit Officer at Emirates NBD Group. He has more than 27 years of experience across banking, aviation, telecommunications and real estate. Previously, Kazim served as Chief Financial Officer at Emirates Integrated Telecommunications Company (du). He also held senior positions at Emirates Group, Meraas and Dubai Airports. In addition, he serves on the Audit Committee of Emirates Development Bank. He is also a member of the UAE Banking Federation Audit Committee. Meanwhile, Iman Al Qasim is Executive Vice President of Human Capital at Emirates Global Aluminium (EGA). She brings more than 20 years of experience in human capital management and organisational transformation. Her previous leadership positions include roles at Emirates National Oil Company (ENOC), Mubadala Investment Company, Dolphin Energy and General Motors Middle East. Al Qasim also serves on the Board of Directors of E7 Group. DP World strengthens corporate governance The appointments add expertise in financial oversight, organisational development and corporate management to DP World’s Board. Essa Kazim, Group Executive Chairman of DP World, welcomed both executives and highlighted their professional backgrounds. “I am pleased to welcome Mr Kazim and Ms Al Qasim to the Board,” said Essa Kazim, Group Executive Chairman of DP World. “Their extensive experience and expertise across a range of industries will bring valuable perspectives to DP World as we continue to strengthen our governance and deliver on our long-term strategic objectives,” he added. The appointments take effect immediately, adding two independent non-executive members to the company’s leadership structure.

articles.title: Russia Says Northern Sea Route Transit Cargo to Nearly Double in 2026
articles.summary: Russia expects cargo transits along the Northern Sea Route (NSR) to more than double in 2026, marking a substantial increase in Arctic shipping despite Western sanctions, although volumes remain far below Moscow’s original ambitions for the route.

(Source: Atomflot via Telegram) Russia expects cargo transits along the Northern Sea Route (NSR) to more than double in 2026, marking a substantial increase in Arctic shipping despite Western sanctions, although volumes remain far below Moscow’s original ambitions for the route. Transit cargo will exceed 7 million tonnes this year, Vladimir Panov, head of the Arctic Directorate at state nuclear corporation Rosatom, said on Oct. 27. Total cargo traffic along the route is expected to surpass 40 million tonnes, also a record, he said. “The Northern Sea Route has two competitive advantages – efficiency and security,” Panov said, adding that the summer-fall route between Asia and Europe is 30% shorter than the passage through the Suez Canal. “Businesses are already voting for the NSR with tonnes,” he said. Transit cargo, which excludes commodities extracted in the Russian Arctic, is a small but growing component of overall traffic. Russia’s forecast of more than 7 million tonnes would nearly double the previous year’s volume, Panov said. Independent tracking by Norway’s Centre for High North Logistics (CHNL) offers a more conservative assessment. By Sept. 30, researchers had identified 104 confirmed transits, already exceeding the 103 recorded during the entire 2025 navigation season. Estimated cargo carried stood at 3.7 million tonnes, compared with 3.2 million tonnes for all of 2025. CHNL estimated that the season could approach 150 transits and exceed 4.5 million tonnes of cargo if most of the voyages already underway at the end of September were completed. The organization’s figures are preliminary estimates based on vessel tracking and available cargo information, rather than official statistics. Oil shipments have been a major driver of this year’s surge. In an unprecedented Arctic operation in August, a convoy of at least 15 vessels, including eight oil tankers, sailed north of the Severnaya Zemlya archipelago to bypass difficult ice conditions in the Vilkitsky Strait . The detour took the ships above 81.5 degrees north, along a route nearly 1,000 kilometers longer than the conventional passage. Russian oil shipments through the NSR had reached approximately 20 million barrels between the start of navigation in July and mid-October, nearly 50% above the previous year’s total. The longer-term picture is equally striking. Total NSR cargo traffic has risen from about 3.7 million tonnes in 2014 to more than 37 million tonnes in each of the past two years, driven overwhelmingly by Russian oil, liquefied natural gas and other resource exports. Yet the growth has fallen well short of the Kremlin’s original targets. President Vladimir Putin had set an 80-million-tonne goal for 2024, before later projecting that annual traffic could reach 70 million to 100 million tonnes by 2030. Russia carried approximately 38 million tonnes in 2024. Western sanctions have delayed or complicated several major Arctic oil and gas developments, limiting the expansion of cargo volumes. Nevertheless, the latest figures demonstrate that Moscow continues to develop the route and redirect trade toward Asian markets, albeit at a slower pace than originally envisioned. It also increasingly relies on sanctioned or shadow fleet vessels to carry goods across the Arctic. Further growth could come from Rosneft’s Vostok Oil project, a major planned oil development on Russia’s Taymyr Peninsula. Increased crude shipments through the Arctic could add substantially to traffic if production and export infrastructure ramp up as planned. Novatek’s LNG exports could also contribute to the shift. The European Union’s planned prohibition on Russian LNG imports under its phaseout schedule, beginning Jan. 1, 2027, is likely to increase pressure on Russian producers to find alternative markets in Asia. The extent to which this translates into additional NSR shipments will depend on production, shipping capacity, ice conditions and available receiving infrastructure. Container shipping is also expanding , although it remains a small part of the route’s overall business. Panov said the number of transit container voyages would rise to 46 this year from 23 in 2025, with international containerized transit cargo expected to exceed 600,000 tonnes. However, those figures have not been independently verified and sit well above what the CHNL observed, which reported just 13 voyages by the end of September. The NSR remains primarily an export corridor for Russian Arctic resources rather than a major alternative to established global shipping lanes. This year’s record figures nevertheless show that sanctions have not halted Russia’s Arctic ambitions. articles.title: Damen orders two additional battery systems from EST-Floattech
articles.summary: Damen Shipyards Group has placed a new order with EST-Floattech for two additional Octopus Series battery systems. The systems will be installed on two Damen Combi Freighter (CF) 3850 cargo vessels. Announced on October 26, the agreement extends the companies’ existing cooperation on battery technology for short-sea...
articles.body: Damen Shipyards Group has placed a new order with EST-Floattech for two additional Octopus Series battery systems. The systems will be installed on two Damen Combi Freighter (CF) 3850 cargo vessels. Announced on October 26, the agreement extends the companies’ existing cooperation on battery technology for short-sea shipping. It also renews their framework agreement, which followed a partnership established in November 2024. With the latest order, the total number of EST-Floattech battery systems installed or planned for installation on CF 3850 vessels will reach nine. The collaboration focuses on improving vessel efficiency and supporting the transition towards lower-emission shipping operations. Damen expands battery integration across cargo vessels The CF 3850 is a cargo vessel designed for short-sea shipping markets. According to Damen, the next-generation version has attracted 50 orders over the past five years. The vessel features an optimised hull design and can accommodate various energy-saving technologies. These options allow operators to improve efficiency while adapting the vessel to their operational requirements. Among the available solutions is the EST-Floattech Octopus battery system. Its capacity ranges from 240 kWh to 1,320 kWh, depending on the configuration selected by the operator. The system can support several onboard functions, including peak shaving and bow thruster operations. Depending on the installed capacity, it can also enable port calls without emissions from onboard power generation during battery-powered operations. By integrating battery storage, vessel operators can reduce reliance on conventional generators during selected operating conditions. “The CF 3850 is a proven vessel with an extensive track record,” said Arjan de Vries, Manager Procurements at Damen Cargo Vessels. De Vries explained that Damen aims to combine its established vessel platform with reliable technologies. He also highlighted the flexibility of the Octopus system, which can be scaled to meet different customer requirements. EST-Floattech strengthens cooperation with Damen The latest order continues a partnership focused on integrating battery storage into commercial cargo vessels. For EST-Floattech, repeated installations on the same vessel design provide opportunities to evaluate system performance and improve future configurations. “We were very pleased to receive this latest order from Damen Cargo Vessels,” said Jelle Meindertsma, Sales Manager at EST-Floattech. Meindertsma highlighted the companies’ ongoing cooperation and the benefits of applying battery technology to an established vessel platform. The Octopus Series is designed to provide modular energy storage solutions for maritime applications. Its flexible configuration allows operators to select battery capacity according to their operational needs. Meanwhile, Damen continues to offer battery integration as part of its wider range of efficiency improvements for the CF 3850. The companies have not disclosed the financial value of the latest order or the specific battery capacities selected for the two vessels. They have also not announced an installation or delivery schedule. Nevertheless, the agreement increases the number of CF 3850 vessels equipped or scheduled to be equipped with EST-Floattech technology, extending the companies’ cooperation in short-sea shipping.

The systems will be installed on two Damen Combi Freighter (CF) 3850 cargo vessels.

articles.summary: The Trump administration announced $498 million in federal grants Tuesday to modernize U.S. ports, funding 35 projects across 19 states ranging from aging dock replacements and cargo-handling equipment to fuel...

Join the leading maritime news network An aerial view of container operations at the Port of Savannah’s Garden City Terminal, where Georgia Ports Authority is expanding capacity amid softer cargo volumes and long-term growth plans. Photo courtesy Georgia Ports The Trump administration announced $498 million in federal grants Tuesday to modernize U.S. ports, funding 35 projects across 19 states ranging from aging dock replacements and cargo-handling equipment to fuel terminal upgrades and advanced maritime monitoring systems. The funding, awarded through the Maritime Administration’s (MARAD) Port Infrastructure Development Program (PIDP), is aimed at improving cargo movement, expanding capacity and strengthening supply chains at coastal seaports, Great Lakes facilities and inland river ports. While significant, the latest round is smaller than the grants awarded in each of the previous four fiscal years. MARAD awarded $774 million to 37 projects in fiscal year 2025, announced this past April, compared with approximately $580 million in 2024, $653 million in 2023 and $703 million in 2022. The new $498 million round is roughly 36% below last year’s total and 26% below the average awarded over the previous four fiscal years. Among the largest recipients is the City of Whittier, Alaska, which will receive $50.6 million to replace the DeLong Dock, install a seasonal floating dock and acquire three pedestal cranes along with an integrated tug and barge. Port Everglades in Florida will receive $30.75 million to strengthen its liquid bulk terminal, widen a slip to accommodate larger vessels and improve resilience to severe weather. The improvements are intended to help maintain critical fuel operations during storms. In North Carolina, the state ports authority will receive $11.25 million for upgrades at the Port of Morehead City, including new heavy-lift cargo infrastructure, crane rails and expanded on-dock rail connections. The project also includes security and cargo-tracking technology. The Red Wing Port Authority in Minnesota will receive $10.2 million to rebuild barge-loading infrastructure along the Mississippi River, including conveyors, an electric winch and dust collection systems. The project will also elevate critical equipment above the river’s floodplain. In Texas, Port Freeport will receive $9.4 million to replace an aging bulk rice loader and expand cargo-handling space, while the Port of Corpus Christi will receive $7.2 million to develop a digital twin of its infrastructure. The Corpus Christi project will incorporate LiDAR, sonar, cameras and other sensing technologies to provide continuous monitoring of port facilities and transportation connections. Smaller projects include nearly $699,000 for Rockport Harbor in Maine to construct a new commercial fishing pier designed to improve transfers of seafood from vessels to trucks. “The strength of our nation’s economy is directly tied to the state of our ports,” Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said. “This nearly half-billion-dollar investment will deliver critical upgrades to ports across America so we can enhance supply chains, lower shipping costs, and create good-paying jobs for hardworking Americans.” MARAD Administrator Stephen Carmel described the awards as part of the administration’s broader maritime revitalization effort. “The President’s commitment to modernizing our port and maritime infrastructure has resulted in an unprecedented investment that will empower local port communities to modernize their operations, integrate innovative technologies, and create safer working environments,” Carmel said. The grants come as one of the federal government’s largest dedicated sources of port infrastructure funding approaches a transition. Much of the current funding stems from the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law signed by President Joe Biden in 2021, which provided $2.25 billion for the PIDP over five years, including $450 million annually from fiscal 2022 through 2026. The Trump administration has proposed maintaining $500 million in PIDP funding for fiscal 2027, including $50 million through regular appropriations and another $450 million through a proposed Maritime Security Trust Fund, a central component of the administration’s maritime revitalization strategy. The investments come as the administration pursues its broader maritime dominance agenda, which includes expanding U.S. shipbuilding capacity, strengthening the merchant marine and modernizing maritime infrastructure. articles.summary: Villa Vie Residences has suspended operations of its residential cruise ship Villa Vie Odyssey in Cambodia, forcing residents to disembark as soaring fuel costs push the company toward financial restructuring....

The vessel has suspended operations in Cambodia amid soaring fuel costs and financial restructuring efforts. Photo: Villa Vie Residences Villa Vie Residences has suspended operations of its residential cruise ship Villa Vie Odyssey in Cambodia, forcing residents to disembark as soaring fuel costs push the company toward financial restructuring. The Fort Lauderdale-based company announced Tuesday that it is evaluating restructuring and recapitalization options over the next 60 days after a sharp increase in fuel expenses made its current operating model financially unsustainable. According to the company, monthly fuel expenses on an equivalent per-cabin basis have surged from a historical average of approximately $1,800 to between $6,000 and $8,000 in parts of Asia, an increase of as much as 344%. The company attributed the increases to the conflict with Iran, which began in late February and has disrupted energy markets and shipping operations worldwide. “Since the conflict began in late February, we have taken significant steps to reduce fuel consumption, including slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port,” the company said. “Those measures have not been enough to offset the extraordinary increase in fuel costs.” The financial pressures have brought an abrupt halt to a voyage that was marketed as a continuous, around-the-world residential cruise. In a notice to residents on Monday, October 26, Villa Vie CEO Kathy Villalba said the company had been unable to secure the fuel needed to continue operating. The vessel would enter temporary layup, with crew remaining aboard to maintain essential systems. Residents were instructed to leave the vessel by 2 p.m. that day, according to a copy of the notice published by resident Randy Cassingham . The company said it is working with residents to coordinate disembarkation and identify temporary living arrangements, acknowledging the disruption for residents, crew members and employees. The shutdown follows earlier efforts to raise additional funding. Cruise Industry News reported that Villa Vie had sought financial contributions from residents, including a recent request for $360,000 to cover fuel expenses. In April, the company reportedly offered residents an emergency loan investment opportunity seeking $3 million, with interest rates ranging from 12% to 24%. It was unclear how much funding, if any, was raised. Cassingham, writing about the shutdown, said the company’s problems extended beyond fuel prices, citing a combination of weaknesses in the business model, management decisions and rising operating expenses. The 195-meter Villa Vie Odyssey , formerly Fred. Olsen Cruise Lines’ Braemar , was acquired by Villa Vie in March 2024 and underwent refurbishment in Belfast before beginning its continuous world voyage in October of that year. The company’s concept offered residents the opportunity to purchase cabins aboard the ship and travel indefinitely, with itineraries taking the vessel to hundreds of destinations around the world. Its Endless Horizons program also offered lifetime cruising through a one-time payment. The financial crisis comes just three months after Villa Vie announced plans for a second residential cruise ship , Legacy , which was expected to enter service in early 2029. At the time, the company said more than 85% of available residences aboard Odyssey had been sold. It also announced plans to extend lifetime residency rights to Legacy and introduced a program allowing new buyers to live aboard Odyssey before transferring to the second vessel. Tuesday’s announcement did not address the future of Legacy or how the suspension might affect residents who purchased cabins or lifetime cruising rights. Villa Vie said it continues to evaluate financing and restructuring alternatives, but no transaction has been finalized and there is no confirmed timetable for resuming operations. The company acknowledged that the outcome of its restructuring efforts remains uncertain. “No outcome is assured,” it said. articles.title: EVI introduces AI safety camera mode to protect seafarer privacy
articles.summary: EVI Safety Technology has launched Crew-First Mode, a new feature for its AI-powered onboard camera system. The technology aims to improve maritime safety while giving seafarers greater protection against routine remote monitoring. The new setting allows the system to detect potential safety risks and alert crew...
articles.body: EVI Safety Technology has launched Crew-First Mode, a new feature for its AI-powered onboard camera system. The technology aims to improve maritime safety while giving seafarers greater protection against routine remote monitoring. The new setting allows the system to detect potential safety risks and alert crew members. At the same time, it limits access to camera footage from shore-based teams. When Crew-First Mode is activated, shore personnel continue to receive safety notifications. However, the associated video footage remains onboard, and routine shore viewing is disabled. According to EVI, the approach allows crews to benefit from AI-assisted safety monitoring without automatically sharing visual records of their activities with shore offices. AI safety monitoring with limits on remote access EVI’s safety technology uses existing onboard cameras to identify potential hazards and notify crew members. This allows personnel to respond to detected risks during vessel operations. The introduction of Crew-First Mode adds another layer of control over how the system handles visual information. Rather than routinely transmitting alert footage to shore-based personnel, the new setting keeps that material onboard. Shore teams can still receive notifications, but they do not have routine access to the corresponding images. The company says this approach addresses concerns about the use of surveillance technology in maritime workplaces. Unlike conventional workplaces, ships also serve as living environments for seafarers. As a result, the use of monitoring equipment raises questions about privacy alongside operational safety. EVI believes safety technology should support crews without creating unnecessary surveillance. “I’ve been a seafarer. I know what it feels like to work under pressure, far from home, with your decisions carrying real consequences,” said Vladimir Ponomarev, CEO of EVI Safety Technology. “If we put cameras around a crew, we owe them more than a promise that the footage will be used responsibly. We have to build those limits into the system,” Ponomarev added. EVI calls for crew-focused maritime technology The launch forms part of EVI’s wider effort to promote greater control over the use of AI-powered monitoring systems at sea. According to the company, technology providers should establish clear limits on who can access footage of seafarers. These restrictions should be built into the systems themselves rather than depend only on internal policies. Crew-First Mode is designed to maintain safety alerts while restricting routine shore access to visual records. The company argues that this approach can help balance the operational benefits of AI monitoring with the privacy expectations of crews. EVI has not disclosed how many vessels currently use Crew-First Mode or whether the feature has been adopted by specific shipping companies. Nevertheless, the launch introduces an additional privacy-focused option for operators considering AI camera systems for onboard safety monitoring.

articles.title: ESAB Launches Rogue ET 230iP AC/DC Welder
articles.summary: ESAB has introduced the Rogue ET 230iP AC/DC TIG/Stick welder. The Rogue combines AC/DC TIG welding capabilities with controls that make it easier for welders of all skill levels to optimize arc performance and weld quality. Featuring ESAB’s 5-in.
articles.body: ESAB Launches Rogue ET 230iP AC/DC Welder Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 27, 2026 © ESAB ESAB has introduced the Rogue ET 230iP AC/DC TIG/Stick welder. The Rogue combines AC/DC TIG welding capabilities with controls that make it easier for welders of all skill levels to optimize arc performance and weld quality. Featuring ESAB’s 5-in. color TFT graphical interface, the Rogue gives operators precise control over heat input, penetration, puddle characteristics and bead appearance without the complexity typically associated with advanced TIG welding systems. Features include pulsed AC and DC TIG outputs, four AC waveshapes, adjustable AC frequency and amplitude offset, and a TIG sequencer. Options include the new CoolMini 3 water-cooler and Heliarc SR-20 water-cooled TIG torch. With Lift TIG and HF arc starting options, Rogue ET 230iP AC/DC enables users to weld steel, stainless steel, aluminum and other metals in a wide range of applications, including general fabrication, process industries, tube and pipe fabrication, repair and maintenance, and aerospace. For optimized arc starts, users enter the tungsten type and diameter, and the machine will automatically set parameters. The Rogue ET 230iP weighs 42 lbs. (without water cooler) and connects to 115/230V AC primary power for location flexibility. It has a TIG welding amperage adjustable from 5 to 230A DC and 15 to 230A AC. On 230V primary, it has a rated TIG output of 230A at 30% duty cycle and a rated Stick output of 180A at 30% duty cycle for welding with electrodes up to 5/32-inch diameter. The Rogue ET 230iP AC/DC works well for welding aluminum because it provides four AC waveshape options: Square for maximum arc stability and energy transfer. Soft square for a softer arc and more fluid puddle. Sinusoidal for a quieter and traditional arc. Triangle for reduced heat input on thinner material. To further tailor the wave form to the application, the machine also offers adjustable amperage offset. The Rogue ET 230iP also provides an AC frequency control adjustable from 50 to 150 Hz. Higher frequencies produce a narrower, more intense arc cone that helps direct the arc at the root of the joint in a fillet weld. Higher frequencies also narrow bead width and increase penetration and travel speeds. The Rogue ET 230iP provides pulsed TIG AC and DC outputs that are adjustable from 0.5 to 200 Hz (pulses per second). With pulsed TIG, the welding power source pulses the welding current between a high peak current and a low background current, with the background current set as a percentage of peak current. Stainless steel fabricators and those working with thin metals or other heat-sensitive applications can use pulsed TIG to control heat input, narrow the weld bead profile and increase travel speed. The machine also offers a new 4T2 mode that switches the value of the main current to a lower welding current with a quick tap of the torch trigger, then returns it with a second tap. This function helps when welding around corners or edges without stopping the weld.

articles.summary: Baleària has floated out its first fully electric fast ferry at Armon Shipyards in Gijón. The vessel will connect Tarifa and Tangier from summer 2027. The second vessel, currently under construction, will join the fleet after the summer. Both catamarans will serve the first green corridor between Spain and Morocco,...
articles.body: Baleària floats out its first fully electric fast ferry, which will connect Tarifa and Tangier from summer 2027 in International Shipping News , Shipping: Emission Possible 27/10/2026 Baleària has floated out its first fully electric fast ferry at Armon Shipyards in Gijón. The vessel will connect Tarifa and Tangier from summer 2027. The second vessel, currently under construction, will join the fleet after the summer. Both catamarans will serve the first green corridor between Spain and Morocco, with an exclusively electric power supply and propulsion system, eliminating emissions, noise and vibrations. Baleària Chairman Adolfo Utor said: “This float-out turns a strategic project for Baleària into a tangible reality and brings us closer to launching the first fully electric maritime connection between Europe and Africa in 2027.” Utor added: “With these vessels, we are bringing forward the 2050 net-zero emissions target by several decades and demonstrating how innovation, investment and industrial collaboration can accelerate the decarbonisation of maritime transport.” For his part, Armón CEO Laudelino Alperi said: “We are proud to contribute our experience and industrial capabilities to such an innovative and emblematic project. Beyond the collaboration between our companies, we want to highlight the excellent personal and professional relationship that unites our teams, built on mutual trust, understanding and a shared commitment. This project reaffirms our commitment to developing increasingly sustainable and technologically advanced marine solutions.” The fast ferry that has just left the dry dock is the fifth vessel built by Armón for Baleària. The shipyard estimates that the two catamarans generate more than 300 direct jobs each day at its facilities, depending on the stage of the project. Construction also generates indirect employment, strengthening the shipbuilding industry’s knock-on effect on supporting industries. The project to build the two vessels and electrify the ports of Tarifa and Tangier City has a cost of more than €200 million. Technological challenge and industrial impact The complexity of the manoeuvre is compounded by the technological challenge. The 87-metre-long vessel has an aluminium structure designed to combine low weight, strength and high performance, while incorporating a high-capacity battery system with 14 MWh of energy storage capacity. The float-out, which involves flooding the dry dock in a controlled manner until the vessel begins to float, is one of the main milestones in the construction process. In this case, the operation also had a distinctive feature: the two catamarans are being built in parallel in the same dry dock, with space for one complete vessel and part of the second. During the float-out of the first vessel, the already assembled structure of its sister ship also became afloat, although it remained in position. Following the float-out, the dock will be drained again so that the second catamaran can be completed in dry conditions. The first vessel, now afloat, will undergo interior outfitting and the gradual commissioning of all its auxiliary systems. (Hanwha General Insurance) signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) with CYTUR Inc. (CYTUR), a company specializing in maritime and vessel cybersecurity, on October 23 to jointly pursue maritime cyber insurance business initiatives. The agreement aims to provide an integrated service combining maritime cyber insurance capabilities with vessel cybersecurity technologies and to actively develop South Korea’s maritime cyber insurance market. As cyber threats targeting maritime supply chains, including attacks on vessel operational technology (OT) systems and disruptions to satellite communications, become a reality, cyber resilience regulations set by the International Maritime Organization (IMO) and the International Association of Classification Societies (IACS) are being strengthened. However, existing vessel insurance policies exclude general cyber-related losses from coverage, leaving shipping companies with significant gaps in coverage. Under the MOU, the two companies have agreed to jointly pursue planning of maritime cyber insurance products and services establishment of cyber threat assessment and cyber resilience-linked systems establishment of a cooperative framework for insurance incident investigations (digital forensics) research into scenario-based loss models. Specifically, CYTUR will assess vessel security levels and provide the technical analysis data required for insurance underwriting, based on its IT/OT cybersecurity technologies covering the entire vessel lifecycle, from design and construction to operation. Even after insurance enrollment, CYTUR plans to continuously monitor vessel security status through its cyber resilience management system and support risk mitigation and reassessments for insurance renewal. In the event of a cyber incident, CYTUR will analyze the cause of the incident and the extent of damage through remote analysis and onboard forensic investigations, and provide technical reports required for insurance incident investigations. Hanwha General Insurance will develop tailored cyber insurance products reflecting the characteristics of the maritime industry and oversee their operation. In particular, the company plans to establish criteria linking vessel security assessment results to insurance eligibility conditions and preferential measures. In the event of a cyber incident, Hanwha General Insurance will operate prompt incident reporting and loss adjustment procedures, and directly establish a cooperative investigation framework, including forensic investigations. The two companies will launch a pilot project and joint marketing activities targeting domestic shipping companies and shipowners in December. They also plan to develop policy-related cooperation initiatives with local governments and classification societies. A spokesperson for Hanwha General Insurance said, “As cyber threats increase rapidly amid the digitalization of vessel operations, our partnership with CYTUR, a cybersecurity specialist, will provide an optimal solution for addressing integrated risk management needs in one place.” The spokesperson added, “Through continued cooperation, the two companies will work together as dependable maritime cyber risk partners to provide differentiated services.” Source: CYTUR Inc. 2026-10-27 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.body: European gas pauses 4-day surge; Depleted storage leaves floor under curves in General Energy News 27/10/2026 European wholesale natural gas prices eased on Tuesday, retreating from fresh 2022 highs touched in the prior session as market participants paused to digest supply disruptions from Norway, though critically depleted regional storage buffers kept a solid structural floor under the curve. Across the North Sea, the British equivalent similarly softened to 238.00 pence per therm, stepping back from Monday’s finish of 239.33 pence as prompt delivery pressure temporarily subsided. Norwegian pipeline disruptions compound geopolitical jitters The minor pullback follows an aggressive surge on Monday driven by unexpected supply curtailments across Europe’s primary pipeline supplier: Norwegian gas network operator Gassco reported an unplanned supply cut at the offshore Oseberg field, escalating an initial outage estimate of 7.7 million cubic meters per day to 12.7 million cubic meters per day. The disruption hit continental trading desks at a delicate moment, abruptly halting pipeline imports just as utilities scrambled to secure physical volumes ahead of seasonal heating demand. Low European storage levels offer little cushion for winter Data from Gas Infrastructure Europe (GIE) shows underground gas storage facilities across the European Union standing at approximately 74.6% of capacity. This marks the lowest inventory level recorded for late October in data dating back to 2009, trailing significantly behind the 86% historical average for this time of year and last year’s 95% fill rates. The structural deficit has been exacerbated by the broader disruption of global maritime flows. The ongoing military escalation involving Iran and Yemen’s Houthis has throttled Liquefied (LNG) shipments transiting through the Strait of Hormuz, leaving Middle Eastern seaborne deliveries to Europe down nearly 80% year-on-year. “The rise in the TTF risk premium is consistent with an increase in perceived Mideast energy supply uncertainty,” Goldman Sachs analysts said. “An increase in tanker attacks near Hormuz earlier this month has kept daily tanker crossing numbers volatile and forward supply highly uncertain.” With cold weather forecasts emerging across Northern Europe for early November, utilities face the prospect of drawing down unseasonably thin reserves earlier than usual, locking European buyers into a fierce bidding war with Asian importers for Atlantic basin cargoes. articles.body: Eurozone bank lending environment showing first hints of tightening in World Economy News 27/10/2026 Adjusted lending to eurozone non-financial corporations continued to grow by 4.2% year-on-year in September, while household lending growth held steady at 3.1%, both unchanged from August. This suggests that the recovery in bank lending that developed before the latest shift in the interest rate environment still had considerable momentum going into the autumn. But the backdrop has now become less supportive. The ECB raised its key rate by 25bp in September, taking the deposit rate to 2.5%, while markets have also repriced the expected rate path higher amid renewed inflation concerns. While September’s lending figures still look healthy, the bank lending survey suggests that eurozone credit growth could moderate. Banks reported a further tightening of credit standards for firms, while corporate loan demand fell unexpectedly in the third quarter as higher interest rates weighed on borrowing. Lending terms tightened across all loan categories, mainly because of higher rates, and a larger share of loan applications was rejected. The survey therefore provides an early indication that tighter monetary conditions are starting to bite: higher borrowing costs are weakening loan demand. The ECB is widely expected to pause on Thursday and wait until December to decide on a possible next hike. With the first signs of more challenging financial conditions coming through and second-round effects of higher energy costs yet to materialise, the ECB will be keen to see how these factors play out before its December meeting. articles.title: DP World joins Canadian partners to explore new Arctic trade corridor

articles.body: DP World, Arctic Gateway Group and CentrePort Canada have signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to explore new trade opportunities across Canada’s northern transportation network. Announced on October 26, 2026, the agreement focuses on port operations, logistics services and the potential development of an integrated trade corridor. The proposed connection would link the Port of Churchill, Hudson Bay Railway, CentrePort Canada and DP World’s global logistics network. The partnership aims to improve access to international markets and strengthen connections between Canada’s inland and coastal transportation infrastructure. It also explores opportunities to connect Europe and Asia through intermodal transportation routes across Canada. Port of Churchill at the centre of proposed trade corridor The Port of Churchill, located on Hudson Bay in northern Manitoba, plays a central role in the proposed partnership. Arctic Gateway Group owns and operates the port and the Hudson Bay Railway. Together, these assets provide a transportation connection between northern Manitoba and the wider Canadian rail network. According to Arctic Gateway Group, the port is handling its most diverse range of commodities to date. These include grain, potash, critical minerals and supplies destined for Nunavut. Meanwhile, discussions are underway to attract private investment for further port modernisation and export growth. The agreement also involves CentrePort Canada, a major inland port and Foreign Trade Zone in Manitoba. Its infrastructure connects businesses through road, rail and air cargo transportation. CentrePort has attracted approximately $1.5 billion in private investment in recent years. More than 1,000 companies operate within the development area. In addition, over 3.5 million square feet of industrial space has been completed or remains under construction over the past eight years. The new partnership will examine how these inland facilities could connect more effectively with Churchill and international shipping networks. DP World to explore logistics connections DP World’s participation brings international port operations and logistics expertise to the initiative. The company handles more than one million TEUs annually in Canada and operates a global network of port terminals and supply chain services. Through the agreement, the three organisations will explore opportunities to improve connections between Canadian exporters and overseas markets. “This agreement is an opportunity to explore how the Port of Churchill, the Hudson Bay Railway and CentrePort Canada can connect more effectively with DP World’s global network and end-to-end logistics capabilities,” said Doug Smith, CEO of DP World in Canada. Smith added that combining the organisations’ infrastructure and expertise could strengthen supply chains and create additional options for Canadian exporters. Chris Avery, President and CEO of Arctic Gateway Group, also highlighted the potential benefits of closer cooperation. According to Avery, better integration between Churchill and Manitoba’s inland transportation infrastructure could support a unified trade corridor. This would help connect Western Canadian resources with new international markets. Carly Edmundson, President and CEO of CentrePort Canada, noted that the partnership could improve access to several existing trade routes. These include the Arctic gateway through Churchill, alongside the Mid-Continent, Asia Pacific and eastern gateways. The agreement comes as Canada seeks to strengthen and diversify its international trade connections. However, the MoU represents an agreement to explore opportunities rather than a confirmed infrastructure investment. The organisations have not announced specific project costs, construction commitments or a timeline for developing the proposed corridor.

The Houthis also said they had attacked Saudi military aircraft and repelled an advance by Saudi-backed forces near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, an important Red Sea shipping route. Intensifying hostilities between Yemen and Saudi Arabia have further disrupted oil supplies and heightened the risk of a wider regional conflict, eight months since the Iran war began. The Houthis' military spokesperson, Yahya Saree, said the strike on the Ras Tanura refinery had caused a fire at the complex, which also includes a shipping terminal and is located on the Gulf, west of the Strait of Hormuz. Saudi authorities did not immediately confirm the strike. Ras Tanura, which has a capacity of 550,000 barrels per day, was shut for a period in the early months of the Iran war as a precautionary measure. Nearly all Saudi Arabia's oil exports flow through two main ports: Ras Tanura in the Gulf and Yanbu on the Red Sea, both of which the Houthis have attacked in the past. Bloomberg News cited a person familiar with the matter as saying Saudi Arabia had contained a fire near Ras Tanura's terminal. AIRSTRIKES The Houthis said they had attacked two military transport jets at Najran Airport and an airbase in Khamis Mushait. There was no immediate Saudi confirmation of the attacks. On Tuesday afternoon, civil defence authorities briefly issued an air raid alert in the Saudi capital Riyadh. The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis in support of Yemen's internationally recognised government said it had intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis towards Riyadh. October has been the worst month for attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and nearby waterways, according to data compiled by a Washington-based think tank that has tracked maritime security incidents worldwide since 2017. articles.title: Oil Tanker Tycoon’s WhatsApp Messages Drive Big Market Moves
articles.summary: The messages from the world’s biggest supertanker owner often begin with pleasantries: “Dear Ladies and Gentlemen.” Within minutes, the WhatsApps are the talk of the oil-tanker industry, a multibillion-dollar corner of the energy market that’s been plunged into chaos by the Iran war this year, and where word of mouth...
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network Photo: Shutterstock/Sven Hansche By Alex Longley, Archie Hunter and Weilun Soon (Bloomberg) — The messages from the world’s biggest supertanker owner often begin with pleasantries: “Dear Ladies and Gentlemen.” Within minutes, the WhatsApps are the talk of the oil-tanker industry, a multibillion-dollar corner of the energy market that’s been plunged into chaos by the Iran war this year, and where word of mouth is the main way information spreads. The details vary, but the messages to shipbrokers from Sinokor Group, the South Korean company controlled by tycoon Ga-Hyun Chung, mostly boil down to the same thing — one of its vessels has just been hired at a new sky-high rate to ferry oil out of the Persian Gulf. Some messages detail a new contract, listing the ship, counterparty and eyewatering price. Others just refer loosely to negotiations underway. The format fluctuates from terse strings of numbers and names to full sentences and florid signoffs: “Very respectfully. Thank you very much and best regards,” concludes one message sent to brokers in August, and seen by Bloomberg. Usually, in the days that follow, the global benchmark price set by London’s Baltic Exchange takes another leap higher. What would simply be fodder for gossip in most industries, brokers say that Sinokor’s WhatsApp messages have for months played an outsized role in setting the cost of transporting oil around the world. Rates for very-large crude carriers — the biggest kind of oil tanker — have soared more than 1,600% this year amid disruptions caused by the war, creating an unprecedented boom for the industry, but throwing a spotlight on the arcane system used to price the world’s shipping contracts, and the centuries-old institution that manages it. The world of oil tanker rates is coming under fresh scrutiny this week, as hearings begin in a London lawsuit brought against the Baltic Exchange by trader Mercuria Energy Group, which argues that the benchmark rate is no longer fit for purpose because of the disruptions caused by the Iran war. Mercuria has complained to the UK’s Financial Conduct Authority about the benchmark, according to its legal filings, and at least one other market participant has also contacted the regulator, according to a person with knowledge of the complaint, who asked not to be identified because it is not public. The Mercuria case doesn’t refer to Sinokor or its role in the market. Mercuria argues that a near-cessation of normal commercial shipments through the Strait of Hormuz since the war began meant that there was no basis on which to calculate the oil tanker market’s most important reference price, known as TD3C, which measures the cost of shipping oil from inside the Persian Gulf to China. But the war is also shining a light on wider questions about how the benchmark is determined, especially as Sinokor’s dominance of the market has expanded. Every day, a select number of shipbrokers submit assessments of the market to the Baltic Exchange, which uses them to publish a price for the TD3C index. While Middle Eastern state producers are having growing success in moving their oil out of the gulf, the trade is still largely covert by nature, reducing the flow of verifiable data. The result, shipowners, traders and brokers say, is that Sinokor’s swaggering Whatsapps are often a key source of information available for assessing the Persian Gulf tanker market, and therefore for setting the global cost of shipping oil. Sinokor has “a huge influence on the market dynamics and the fundamentals of what’s happening on the VLCC market,” said Joel Grau, chief executive officer at shipping insurer Zostera Marine and a professor at the National Maritime College of Ireland. To be sure, the tanker market is being supported by a genuine supply squeeze, with more vessels tied up on longer and unusual routes or waiting to collect oil outside the gulf, and as Iran escalates missile and drone strikes on ships. But nearly two decades after uproar over the Libor rate of borrowing, the scrutiny of the Baltic Exchange’s main tanker rate is once again raising questions over the reliability of a financial benchmark that prices billions of dollars in derivatives and is set not by trades but by the assessments of market participants. “I will of course still carry out my duties, but have we (the Baltic) taken any legal advice on the questionable market situation,” Christopher Loveday, an assessor for TD3C at the Baltic Exchange, asked a colleague in mid-March, according to a Mercuria legal filing. He expressed concern that the Baltic could face “issues” with market participants “like the Libor situation a decade or so ago,” according to the filing. (There’s no suggestion in Mercuria’s legal filings that the wrongdoing that led to the Libor scandal is at play at the Baltic Exchange, nor has any regulator or other party suggested as such.) The importance of TD3C itself is already being eroded. Open interest on the underlying derivatives contracts has declined, and industry insiders say they’re increasingly focused on a new Baltic index called TD34 that prices the cost of shipping oil from just outside of the Strait of Hormuz to Asia. This story is based on interviews with over a dozen people involved in oil tanker markets, most of whom asked not to be identified discussing private interactions and business dealings. Sinokor didn’t respond to requests for comment. The Baltic Exchange and Mercuria declined to comment. The FCA said it can’t comment on engagement with individual firms and that it has been monitoring the impact of the Iran war since the conflict began. In its defense, the Baltic Exchange, which is owned by Singapore Exchange Ltd., has said that its decision to keep publishing TD3C wasn’t taken lightly. Mercuria is asking the court to retroactively suspend the index. However, the Baltic’s lawyers said that doing so would mean dissolving more than eight months of pricing and that “such a claim is without precedent in this jurisdiction or, to the Baltic’s knowledge, in any other.” It was barely two weeks into the Iran war, on March 12, when brokers received a notification from Sinokor that it had hired out a ship to sail from the United Arab Emirates port of Zirku to Asia at a rate of at least 700 Worldscale points — far above the Baltic’s assessment for that day of 348.89. The Worldscale system is a standardized way of comparing tanker freight rates across different routes. At the time, prices had already been soaring for months after Sinokor, until then a relatively smaller player, suddenly embarked on a massive supertanker buying spree with backing from container shipping giant MSC Mediterreanean Shipping Co. The aggressive move gave Chung — the deeply private scion of a Korean shipping family — a level of influence in the tanker market that insiders say is unprecedented, and meant that Sinokor was positioned to reap huge profits when the war started. By the time of Sinokor’s March WhatsApp, the Baltic Exchange was facing turmoil of its own, as shipbrokers grappled with how to calculate the cost of shipping from a Saudi Arabian port that was effectively inaccessible due to the war. Some began using a still-functioning Saudi port on the Red Sea for their TD3C assessments, but the exchange intervened and insisted that the benchmark price must continue to reflect loadings from inside the Persian Gulf. By March 16, the Baltic’s rate jumped to almost 600 Worldscale points, equivalent to $602,000 a day, as traders struggled to assess a trade that appeared to have stalled, and with barely any visibility of deals being done other than Sinokor’s notice. Prices continued to swing wildly in the coming weeks, and in late April Mercuria filed a lawsuit alleging that it had suffered losses in the hundreds of millions of dollars as a result of distortions in the benchmark, though its lawyers said in May that it was not looking to “extract money from an exchange.” The company since removed the figure from its claim. Mercuria argues that the index should be suspended immediately, and that since the Iran war began the route no longer serves its intended function. For its part, the Baltic’s argues that would be an unprecedented move and that if that request were granted there would be “chaotic market-wide consequences,” including for the multibillion-dollar derivatives market linked to TD3C. For decades, the Baltic Exchange’s Middle East to Asia benchmark has stood at the heart of the oil tanker market, used as a reference point in long-term contracts for supertanker deals — including for vessels sailing elsewhere in the world — and underpinning a large derivatives market. The original TD3 route measured the cost of traveling to Japan, but was replaced about a decade ago with TD3C, to reflect China’s growing dominance as an oil importer. The rate is published just after 4 p.m. London time every day, based on the average of assessments provided by nine brokers. The individual brokers submit their estimates shortly before the price is issued, although the Baltic Exchange can occasionally ask for justification for the figures, one of the people said. Mercuria’s lawsuit alleged that TD3C was being distorted, and its lawyers argued that the handful of ships transiting Hormuz in the early months of the war should not qualify as fixtures for setting the benchmark rate. By the summer, however, the flow of oil out of the Persian Gulf was becoming a steady stream, as producers and traders settled into a new “dark shuttle” system — using dedicated tankers making return journeys under cover of night before offloading oil onto ships waiting empty just outside the gulf. Bloomberg reported in early July that Sinokor had emerged as a major owner of supertankers moving crude through the strait of Hormuz. But the level of information about ships and cargoes operating in the region for the most part remained extremely limited. It was around that time that the Sinokor messages — referred to among industry insiders as “blasts” — began to accelerate. Sinokor owner Chung already had a reputation in shipping circles for creating sprawling WhatsApp groups with representatives from individual brokerage firms or counterparties, usually including large numbers of Sinokor employees as well. In late July, when TD3C had begun to retreat following the interim peace deal between the US and Iran that notionally lowered the risk of attack in Hormuz, Sinokor “blasted” out that it had hired out a ship at 465 Worldscale points, about 60 points higher than where the market was assessed that day. The difference is the equivalent to just over $60,000 a day in earnings. Sinokor sent out at least five missives in August, each announcing progressively higher rates. By Aug. 21, the company told the market that it hired a ship out at 1,350 Worldscale points, almost three times the level of just under a month earlier. In the months to come, the market went parabolic, surging from around 400 points in late July, to almost 1,320 points in October. Supertankers in the Persian Gulf — and any deals still tied to TD3C— were now earning more than $1.4 million a day. The potential payoff for Sinokor and its partner MSC is huge. Sinokor is listed as the manager of 83 supertankers on the Equasis maritime database, many of which are operating in or around the Middle East. Most industry figures see the company controlling more vessels than that in reality when charter deals are added in too. Using a gauge of average supertanker earnings across the world, a fleet of 83 ships would have pulled in on average of about $143 million a month last year. That jumped to $509 million by July this year, $1.4 billion in September, and $2.1 billion in October, based on the average for the month so far. In reality, it depends where the vessels are sailing, and those figures don’t account for costs and days where ships aren’t hired. (Some of the company’s ships have been hit in Hormuz recently, potentially reducing the number of days its tankers can earn money while they undergo repairs.) By comparison, Sinokor’s revenue for the whole of 2025, which also includes a container shipping arm, was $5.5 billion, according to accounts published in South Korea. While the financial rewards for companies like Sinokor willing to take the risk of crossing Hormuz are significant, the journeys also ultimately provided a vital lifeline to global energy markets. Worst case-scenario forecasts of $200 a barrel crude oil prices never materialized, partly as a result of the ships that continued to cross Hormuz. Sinokor itself carried an estimated 37% of the oil that passed through the Strait of Hormuz last month, Bloomberg reported last week. For many in the industry, the crucial question is how literally to take the Sinokor messages, which have become less frequent since the summer. Several people involved in tanker markets said Sinokor’s WhatsApps can leave room for interpretation around parts of the rate being publicized, like who pays for insurance, or the ship’s destination. And the already opaque shipping market has become even harder to track as a result of the Iran war, as most ships in the Middle East have stopped broadcasting satellite signals that make their movements easy to follow. Tracking and satellite images show that while some of the bookings the company broadcast went exactly as advertised, others are less clear. At least one ship that Sinokor said would sail from the Middle East to Asia in early August hasn’t left the Indian Ocean and Persian Gulf since then. To be sure, charterers and shipowners will sometimes privately agree to change the route they’re due to sail, while bookings can also fall through. The Baltic Exchange’s policies say that panelists should use discretion over the relative value they attribute to data they gather and — in cases where there is little or no activity on a route for a period of time — must apply their “expert judgement of the wider market” to provide an assessment. Of 130 published days between early March and early September, the Baltic Exchange said in its defense that there were 12 instances where one broker didn’t provide the Baltic with an assessment for the route, citing difficulties in assessing the market. Last month, a different broker said that it would no longer input data for the route on an indefinite, but temporary basis, the exchange added in its defense for the court case. “There is an element of trust when you are determining the price of shipping oil,” said Halvor Ellefsen, a London-based director at Fearnleys Shipbrokers UK Ltd. “With such a dominant player making bullish uncorroborated proclamations, although lacking underlying contractual details, it has never been more difficult to figure out where in reality TD3C sits. TD34 has by and large taken over from TD3C as a reliable benchmark.” © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. articles.title: Russia Ships Less Crude Even as Key Baltic Port’s Flows Rebound
articles.summary: Russia shipped the least crude in more than a month, even as operations at its key Baltic port recovered strongly from an earlier halt.
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. REUTERS/Tatiana Meel (Bloomberg) — Russia shipped the least crude in more than a month, even as operations at its key Baltic port recovered strongly from an earlier halt. In the four weeks through Oct. 25, overseas crude flows edged lower to 3.55 million barrels a day, tanker data compiled by Bloomberg showed. That was down by 30,000 barrels a day from the period to Oct. 18, to the lowest in five weeks. The drop came despite a rebound in weekly flows. A total of 12 tankers left the Primorsk terminal near St. Petersburg last week. That compared with just four the previous week, which saw a three-day gap in arrivals and departures. Similar interruptions in the past were linked to maintenance. Russia’s war on Ukraine is hitting global supplies of fuel and food, compounding the impact of the conflict in the Persian Gulf and sending crude prices to the highest since the early days of the full-scale invasion, when the Brent benchmark briefly topped $120 a barrel. A recent lull in Kyiv’s attacks on Russian refineries has allowed Moscow to boost processing rates, likely diverting crude that would otherwise have been exported. There were no reported strikes on Russian oil processing plants in the seven days to Oct. 25, amid moves to initiate trilateral talks between Russia, Ukraine and the US. If the halt to attacks on refineries continues, the amount of Russian crude available for export could fall in the coming weeks, as previously damaged plants are repaired and brought back into operation. At the same time, buyers in India may be turning away from Russian barrels amid sky-high shipping costs and cheaper alternatives from the Persian Gulf. The shift comes as crude flows from the Middle East return to near pre-war levels. Whether those flows can be maintained if the Iran conflict flares up after the US mid-terms and the Israeli election remains to be seen. In the week to Oct. 25, some 37 tankers loaded 26.93 million barrels of Russian crude, vessel-tracking data and industry reports show. The volume compared with a slightly revised 21.87 million barrels on 31 ships the previous week. Shipments jumped by 730,000 barrels a day last week to average 3.85 million barrels a day, the highest in a month. Flows from Primorsk rebounded after a gap in ship movements of several days during the previous week that suggested that loading operations may have been suspended for maintenance at the port or the pipeline that supplies it. Weekly shipments can be volatile, affected by weather, maintenance work, sanctions, military activity and the timing of departures. There was one shipment of Kazakhstan’s Kebco grade from Novorossiysk during the week. Since the start of September, Moscow has diverted all shipments of Kazakh crude through the Black Sea port, freeing up more capacity for its own barrels at Ust-Luga on the Baltic, which is seen as safer. The amount of Russian crude on the water rebounded last week, driven by the jump in shipments from the country’s Baltic ports. On a four-week average basis, the gross value of Moscow’s oil shipments was little changed at $2.61 billion a week in the 28 days to Oct. 25, close to the previous week’s three-week low. The small drop in total flows and lower prices for Russia’s key Urals crude were offset by higher prices for the Pacific ESPO grade. On a weekly basis, the value of exports jumped by about $430 million to a wartime high of $2.76 billion, with lower Urals prices more than offset by the jump in shipments and an eighth straight weekly increase in ESPO values. China and India remain the biggest buyers of Russian crude by a considerable margin. But it’s not always possible to assign a final destination to individual cargoes until well into their voyage, leaving many of the more recent shipments on tankers showing interim destinations, such as Suez, Port Sudan, or Singapore. These are recorded as “Unknown Asia” until a credible final destination is available. Ships still showing their destinations as their Russian loading ports, or places such as Gibraltar, are recorded as “Other Unknown.” Observed shipments to Russia’s Asian customers, including those showing no final destination, edged lower to to 3.42 million barrels a day in the 28 days to Oct. 25, down from a revised 3.45 million in the period to Oct. 18. Shipments to Moscow’s remaining customers in the Mediterranean region were unchanged from the revised figure for the period to Oct. 18. That figure was revised down to about 130,000 barrels a day after one tanker heading toward Turkey changed its destination to the Suez Canal. That took flows to Turkey to about 80,000 barrels a day in the four weeks to Oct. 25, unchanged from the earlier period. An earlier flurry of shipments to Egypt, which took flows to as much as 160,000 barrels a day in mid-June, has fallen back to about 50,000 barrels a day in the most recent period. Flows to Syria have fallen to zero since August after the Mediterranean nation agreed to “drastically” reduce Russian oil imports in negotiations with the US on lifting remaining sanctions. Shipments to the region may be revised higher once destinations for almost 1.8 million barrels a day of crude become clear. Historically, most cargoes on ships showing intermediate destinations have been delivered to India or China. Photo courtesy Port of Los Angeles A labor dispute involving port watchmen could disrupt operations at eight marine terminals in the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach as early as November 1, just weeks after the nation’s busiest container port complex reported record cargo volumes. The International Longshore and Warehouse Union (ILWU) Local 26 has warned fellow maritime unions that its members may go on strike when the latest extension of their labor agreement expires on Sunday. In an October 23 letter, Local 26 President Luisa Gratz said the union has been engaged in unsuccessful contract negotiations with employers and the Pacific Maritime Association (PMA) since 2025. “Although PMA has recently requested Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service’s participation, and Local 26 agreed, nothing of value has resulted from the Union’s commitment to bargaining in good faith with our employers and PMA,” Gratz wrote. The union said it has been operating under a series of contract extensions since last year, with the latest set to expire November 1. The eight affected terminal locations are APM Terminals (APMT), Long Beach Container Terminal (LBCT), Total Terminals International (TTI), SSA at C-60, A-90, LB 206, Pacific Container Terminal (PCT), and OH 55. The strike threat comes at a particularly busy time for the Southern California ports. Los Angeles and Long Beach both set all-time monthly cargo records in September , handling a combined 2.04 million twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs) as strong imports and shifting global trade patterns drove cargo through the complex. The record volumes capped an unusually extended peak shipping season that has stretched well into the fall. However, the National Retail Federation expects imports to slow as the holiday shipping rush winds down, forecasting volumes at major U.S. container ports to decline from 2.25 million TEUs in October to 2 million in November. Local 26 represents maritime security employees and watchmen responsible for security-related duties at marine terminals, including gate and cargo watch operations. Their labor agreement is separate from the broader coastwide contract covering ILWU longshore workers and marine clerks, which runs through 2028. The PMA was also at the center of the last major West Coast port labor dispute in 2023, when contentious negotiations with the ILWU led to work slowdowns and terminal shutdowns at several ports, including Los Angeles and Long Beach. That dispute ended with a six-year coastwide agreement covering approximately 22,000 workers at 29 West Coast ports. While the current dispute involves a smaller bargaining unit, it raises the possibility of wider disruptions if picket lines affect terminal access or other maritime workers decline to cross them. In her letter, Gratz appealed directly to other maritime unions for support. “This letter shall serve as a preliminary notice of a problem and visible labor dispute, which will affect your members,” she wrote. “We are asking for your support and labor solidarity in respect for Local 26 Watchmen on the identified Marine Terminals in Long Beach and Los Angeles Harbor.” The International Organization of Masters, Mates & Pilots (MM&P), which represents licensed deck officers aboard U.S.-flag vessels, said it would provide further guidance to members working at affected berths as the deadline approaches. The notice does not confirm that a strike will take place, and the extent of any potential disruption remains unclear. REUTERS/Francis Mascarenhas Global marine insurance premiums rose 5.5% to $42.6 billion in 2025, but increased competition, excess capacity and currency fluctuations continued to weigh on the market, according to a new report from the International Union of Marine Insurance (IUMI). The figures, published Tuesday in IUMI’s annual Stats Report , show premium growth across most major insurance lines, supported by expanding global fleets, higher vessel values and rising demand for war risk coverage. However, IUMI cautioned that much of the reported growth reflected the weaker U.S. dollar rather than an underlying strengthening of market conditions. Ocean hull insurance premiums increased 9.4% to $10.5 billion, driven by fleet expansion, higher ship values and additional war premiums. Even so, fleet growth continued to outpace premium growth, pointing to sustained competitive pressure on insurers. Marine cargo insurance remained the largest segment, with premiums rising 6.9% to $24.2 billion. Growth was supported by seaborne trade and changes in commodity and asset values, particularly in China, where exports of high-value technology, including AI-related equipment and semiconductors, helped drive demand. Offshore energy insurance premiums were virtually unchanged at $4.82 billion, an increase of just 0.1%. London retained its dominant position with a 62.7% market share, including a growing renewables component. “The 2025 marine insurance market recorded modest growth in global premiums, although underlying conditions remained soft,” said IUMI Secretary General Lars Lange. “Increased capacity, competitive pressures and currency movements, particularly the weakness of the US dollar, all influenced reported premium levels.” Claims activity remained relatively stable during 2025, with no single catastrophic event significantly affecting an individual insurance sector. However, the accumulation of smaller claims continued to pressure profitability. Looking ahead, IUMI warned that geopolitical tensions are playing an increasingly important role in marine insurance markets in 2026, particularly as the conflict in the Middle East disrupts shipping and increases demand for war risk coverage. War insurance has become increasingly prominent as attacks on commercial shipping continue, while the availability of energy carriers has tightened amid heightened security risks in the region. “Looking ahead, geopolitical tensions continued to shape the market into 2026,” Lange said. “War cover became increasingly prominent while vessel availability, particularly for energy carriers, tightened as conflict in the Middle East intensified.” Despite concerns that tariffs would significantly constrain international trade, IUMI said the impact had been less severe than initially anticipated, while global economic growth exceeded expectations. Asia continued to lead growth in the marine insurance market, with China remaining the region’s largest contributor. European markets also expanded, although at a slower pace. The report also updates IUMI’s Major Claims Database, which now includes approximately 7,200 cargo claims representing a cumulative $11.4 billion in losses. Thirty national insurance associations contribute to the database, which tracks claims dating back to 2013. IUMI also introduced a revised Hull Inflation Index designed to help insurers assess rising vessel repair costs using broader economic indicators. articles.title: Hanwha General Insurance, CYTUR to Explore Maritime Cyber Insurance Initiatives
articles.summary: Hanwha General Insurance Co., Ltd. signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) with CYTUR Inc., a company specializing in maritime and vessel cybersecurity, on October 23 to jointly pursue maritime cyber insurance business initiatives. The agreement…
articles.body: Hanwha General Insurance, CYTUR to Explore Maritime Cyber Insurance Initiatives Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 27, 2026 © Hanwha General Insurance Co. Hanwha General Insurance Co., Ltd. signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) with CYTUR Inc., a company specializing in maritime and vessel cybersecurity, on October 23 to jointly pursue maritime cyber insurance business initiatives. The agreement aims to provide an integrated service combining maritime cyber insurance capabilities with vessel cybersecurity technologies and to actively develop South Korea's maritime cyber insurance market. As cyber threats targeting maritime supply chains, including attacks on vessel operational technology (OT) systems and disruptions to satellite communications, become a reality, cyber resilience regulations set by the International Maritime Organization (IMO) and the International Association of Classification Societies (IACS) are being strengthened. However, existing vessel insurance policies exclude general cyber-related losses from coverage, leaving shipping companies with significant gaps in coverage. Under the MOU, the two companies have agreed to jointly pursue Planning of maritime cyber insurance products and services Establishment of cyber threat assessment and cyber resilience-linked systems Establishment of a cooperative framework for insurance incident investigations (digital forensics) Research into scenario-based loss models. Specifically, CYTUR will assess vessel security levels and provide the technical analysis data required for insurance underwriting, based on its IT/OT cybersecurity technologies covering the entire vessel lifecycle, from design and construction to operation. Even after insurance enrollment, CYTUR plans to continuously monitor vessel security status through its cyber resilience management system and support risk mitigation and reassessments for insurance renewal. In the event of a cyber incident, CYTUR will analyze the cause of the incident and the extent of damage through remote analysis and onboard forensic investigations, and provide technical reports required for insurance incident investigations. Hanwha General Insurance will develop tailored cyber insurance products reflecting the characteristics of the maritime industry and oversee their operation. In particular, the company plans to establish criteria linking vessel security assessment results to insurance eligibility conditions and preferential measures. In the event of a cyber incident, Hanwha General Insurance will operate prompt incident reporting and loss adjustment procedures, and directly establish a cooperative investigation framework, including forensic investigations. The two companies will launch a pilot project and joint marketing activities targeting domestic shipping companies and shipowners in December. They also plan to develop policy-related cooperation initiatives with local governments and classification societies.

Join the leading maritime news network Photo: Tommy Alven/Shutterstock Swedish shipping group Stena AB has agreed to acquire Norwegian ferry operator Color Line, bringing together two of Scandinavia’s largest ferry companies in a deal that would significantly expand Stena’s presence in the European passenger and freight markets. The acquisition, announced Monday , is subject to regulatory approval and is expected to close in late first quarter or during the second quarter of 2027. Financial terms were not disclosed. Under the agreement, Stena AB’s subsidiary Stena Rederi AB will acquire all shares in Color Group AS from ONS Invest II AS, which is owned by Norwegian industrialist Olav Nils Sunde and his family. The transaction would bring Color Line’s five-vessel fleet and four international ferry routes under the same ownership as Stena Line, one of Europe’s largest ferry operators, with 40 ships operating across 19 routes in Northern Europe and the Mediterranean. Color Line operates services connecting Norway with Germany, Denmark and Sweden, including the Oslo–Kiel route served by its large cruise ferries Color Magic and Color Fantasy . Its other services connect Kristiansand and Larvik with Hirtshals, Denmark, and Sandefjord with Strömstad, Sweden. In 2025, Color Line carried nearly 3.6 million passengers and 150,000 freight units, generating revenue of more than NOK 6.7 billion ($700 million approximately). Stena Line, meanwhile, operates approximately 35,000 sailings annually, carrying passengers and freight across an extensive European network. The company reported revenue of SEK 20.2 billion and employs approximately 8,750 people. The combination would strengthen Stena’s position in Scandinavian ferry transport while adding Color Line’s established Norwegian operations to its broader European network. “This is a true milestone in Stena Line’s history,” said Niclas Mårtensson, CEO of Stena Line, describing the acquisition as an opportunity to expand the companies’ operations and contribute to tourism and more sustainable shipping. Despite the change in ownership, Stena said it intends to preserve Color Line as a separate business, retaining its existing brand, Norwegian management and Norwegian-registered fleet. The Swedish group also plans to support further investment in fleet decarbonization, technology, digitalization, customer service and freight logistics. Color Line CEO Trond Kleivdal welcomed the agreement, saying Stena’s ownership would provide a stronger foundation for the Norwegian operator’s future development while preserving its established market position. The companies said there would be no immediate changes to ferry schedules, bookings or existing customer and supplier relationships. Both operators will continue running independently while the transaction undergoes regulatory review. The proposed acquisition marks a significant consolidation in the Northern European ferry industry, bringing together two longstanding family-owned maritime businesses with complementary route networks and substantial passenger and freight operations.
